newsitem.title: ITALY: Friends of accused protest in Italy child-sex case.
newsitem.headline: Friends of accused protest in Italy child-sex case.

text.p: About 100 people set fire to litter bins and stopped traffic in the southern Italian city of Naples on Thursday in protest at the arrest of 17 friends and relations on suspicion of running a child pornography ring.

Police said the demonstrators set fire to rubbish and tyres in a park, halted traffic for an hour and waved banners denouncing investigators and the media for what they considered to be sensationalism in the case, which has shocked Italy.
They claimed many of the 17 detainees were innocent of child abuse and said the allegations had been blown out of proportion. Police said the crowd finally ended its protest peacefully.

The 17 were arrested on Tuesday and are being held in preventative detention on suspicion of raping and assaulting 19 children aged between six and nine in the rundown Naples suburb of Torre Annunziata.
They are also suspected of drugging and chaining up the children while using them to make pornographic videos.
The case has caused profound shock in Italy, famed for its family values, and comes hard on the heels of a recent spate of horrific child sex revelations in Belgium and France.

French authorities have placed more than 300 people under investigation and remanded more than 20 in custody in the last few days in a nationwide inquiry into the sale of pornographic video cassettes involving under-age boys.
Anna Serafini, vice-president of the justice commission of Italy's lower house of parliament, said on Thursday an "anti-paedophiles" draft law should be approved within weeks.
"A law on sexual abuse on its own is not enough to beat the phenomenon of paedophilia, but in the meantime, let's pass it," she told a conference in Naples.
The popularly-dubbed "anti-paedophiles" law would introduce severe punishments for sex abuse against children and Serafini said it was likely to become law before the end of the summer.
But she said a law on sex education was also needed to "warn children of the risks they run".
The Italian government has opened an investigation alongside the inquiry by local magistrates into the Torre Annunziata affair.
"We want to know everything," said Education Minister Luigi Berlinguer. "We cannot wait even one day because certain crimes cannot be left unpunished."
Investigations into the ring began more than a year ago after the mother of one of the children went to the police.

Prosecutor Aldredo Ormanni told reporters this week that some of the children were assaulted at school. The detainees included several women and a primary school caretaker, who was suspected of helping to lure the children away during recreation time with promises of pocket money.
Newspapers quoted some mothers of children at the school on Thursday as saying that a Mafia-like code of silence had prevented the situation from emerging earlier.
